column4: Salih names نَاقَةُ ٱللَّهِ as a sign, tells Thamud to let her eat on God's earth, and explicitly says not to touch her with harm; this is the expanded warning compressed into 91:13's camel and watering-right formula.
Salih again identifies God's she-camel as a sign, grants her access to God's earth, and warns his people not to harm her, making the protected animal and its divinely assigned use explicit.
Salih assigns the she-camel one drinking turn and the people a known day's turn, the clearest parallel to the section's claim that سُقيا is a protected, apportioned right.
The next instruction, not to touch the she-camel with harm, spells out the warning carried by the accusatives in 91:13 and ties violation of her water-share to the threatened punishment.
God orders Salih to announce that the water is divided between camel and people and that every drinking turn is attended, directly joining provision, partition, and enforceable entitlement.
Twelve springs burst from the stone and every group knows its own مَشْرَب; the command to eat and drink from God's provision makes an ordered water-share a divine gift and duty.
The twelve tribes and twelve springs repeat the same scene: every people knows its drinking place, so communal difference is sustained by a divinely organized water allocation.

ذَنُوبًا gives wrongdoers a portion like the portions of their predecessors; it is the Quranic use behind the source dictionary's “bucket/share” sense and turns punishment into the exact share awaiting them.

God's inward communication to Moses' mother immediately commands her to suckle him; divine inspiration and a young one's taking milk meet in one ayah, just as the section explains inward inspiration through nursing.

Thamud mockingly asks whether the reminder was “cast” upon one man among them; أَأُلْقِىَ ٱلذِّكْرُ closely stages the source dictionary's image of something cast inward, inside the very passage that proceeds to the camel and her water.
God says He is sending the she-camel as a trial and commands watchful patience; the sent animal, the messenger-root resonance, and the test of honoring her assigned share converge here.
The river tests Saul's troops by a precisely limited drink—abstention except for one hand-scoop—showing water consumption itself becoming a measured moral trial.
God holds the treasuries of everything and sends each thing down only in a known measure, supplying the hidden reserve and exact allotment that the section hears in an assigned drink.
God sends water and فَأَسْقَيْنَاكُمُوهُ, while humans do not hold its stores; the same س ق ي family presents drinking as something God makes available from a reserve He controls.
Water descends “in measure,” is lodged within the earth, and can be taken away, concretely joining a measured share, a hidden store, and the giver's continuing control.
God gives drink from cattle's bellies as pure milk pleasant to drinkers; it realizes both the source's suckling image and its secondary رَسْل sense of abundant flowing milk.
Those who accept guidance receive increased guidance and are given تَقْوَاهُمْ; this directly parallels the soul's receiving its taqwa from God in 91:8.

God makes faith beloved and beautiful in believers' hearts while making disbelief, فسوق, and disobedience hateful, an explicit inward presentation of opposed moral possibilities akin to the soul taking in fujur and taqwa.
Gabriel brings revelation down upon the Prophet's heart by God's permission, a direct Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's description of a God-given thing entering inward awareness.
Revelation comes عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ so that the Prophet may warn; the heart is explicitly the receiving vessel for what descends from God.
Every نَفْس tastes death and is tested with both evil and good; tasting and the paired test make the soul itself an ingesting subject for contrary allotments.

Those who take a measure from others يَسْتَوْفُونَ—take it in full—echo the source dictionary's form استوفاه for the young animal exhausting the udder and expose the injustice of securing one's whole share.
The same people diminish what they measure out to others, a precise ethical reversal of taking one's own full portion while obstructing the camel's allotted portion.
God says each destroyed people was seized بِذَنۢبِهِۦ and then names their differing destructions, directly presenting sin as the individualized cause and measure of the share received.

Thamud hamstring the she-camel, defy their Lord's command, and challenge Salih to bring the threatened punishment, connecting violation of the protected share to the people's demand for their own consequence.
The earthquake seizes the people after the hamstringing, supplying the punishment side of the section's exchange between the camel's denied portion and their resulting portion.
After hamstringing the camel, the people receive a precisely bounded three-day respite, so even the interval before their promised consequence is measured out.
The blast seizes the wrongdoers after they violate the camel warning, repeating the immediate passage from denied animal right to received punishment.
They hamstring the she-camel and then become regretful, the decisive act that converts a divided water arrangement into culpability.
The punishment takes them immediately after the hamstringing, completing the same action-and-recompense sequence condensed in 91:13–14.
Thamud call their companion, who takes action and hamstrings the sent she-camel; this is the concrete breach of the water test announced in 54:27–28.
God asks how His punishment and warnings were, marking the consequence as the answer to the camel test and its rejected warning.
A single blast leaves them like crushed pen-stalks, giving the physical result of violating the apportioned water arrangement.
God says He gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign and they wronged her; the whole water-right episode is named as a divinely supplied sign met by injustice.
Like Pharaoh's people and those before them, rejecters are seized بِذُنُوبِهِمْ; the same phrase as 91:14 ties communal destruction to sins as the share that occasions it.
Earlier, materially stronger generations are destroyed بِذُنُوبِهِمْ and replaced, another direct use of sins as the cause of a fully delivered communal consequence.
Pharaoh's house and earlier peoples are seized بِذُنُوبِهِمْ after rejecting God's signs, repeating the exact causal vocabulary of the section's punishment-share.
The same comparison culminates in “We destroyed them for their sins” and Pharaoh's people are drowned, pairing the root ذ ن ب with a water-borne destruction.
Powerful former peoples are seized بِذُنُوبِهِمْ with no protector from God, making their worldly strength unable to alter their assigned consequence.
The speaker says the نَفْس persistently commands evil except where the Lord grants mercy, locating fujur-like pressure within the soul while preserving God's decisive gift.
The one who fears standing before the Lord restrains the نَفْس from desire, showing the enacted taqwa-side of the soul's two inward possibilities.
Every نَفْس is held in pledge for what it earns, joining the soul as recipient with the individualized moral share produced by its acts.
God says He inspired the disciples to believe in Him and His messenger; divine inward prompting, its moral content, and رَسُول meet explicitly.
Moses is to be cast into the chest and river, while God says He cast love upon him from Himself; physical casting and a God-given inward quality overlap with the dictionary image behind ilham.
After the bee receives divine inspiration, a healing drink of varied colors emerges from its belly; inward divine direction and a drink held within a creature form a single sequence.
Mothers are to suckle children for two complete years, with support apportioned by recognized fairness; nursing, full completion, and measured responsibility all sharpen the source's suckling image.
Moses reaches a water source where shepherds are watering their flocks while two women hold theirs back, staging access to a shared animal-watering place and its social ordering.
Moses waters the women's flock for them—فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا—an exact concrete instance of س ق ي as giving another creature what it drinks.
God sends sky-water from which people drink and vegetation grows for grazing, uniting the animal's drink, its pasture, and divine provision.
Livestock are a lesson because God gives people drink from what is within their bellies and also grants other benefits and food, directly extending the udder-and-ingestion scene.
Rain revives dead land and God gives it as drink to livestock and many people, placing herd and human drinking under one act of divine provision.
Abraham identifies God as the One who feeds him and gives him drink, stating the giver-recipient relation that the section unfolds through سُقيا.
God sends sky-water بِقَدَرٍ and revives dead land, presenting water itself as a measured allotment whose quantity and life-giving effect belong to Him.
Had people remained straight on the way, God says He would have given them abundant water to drink; water provision is explicitly linked to moral stance.
The abundant water of the previous ayah is itself a test, clarifying that a generous drink-share, like the camel's, can expose obedience rather than merely satisfy need.
God sets firm mountains and gives people sweet water to drink, another direct use of س ق ي for an inhabitable world's allotted provision.
God makes every living thing from water, closely matching the source dictionary's claim that water can be called nafs because the living self subsists by it.
God creates and proportionates—خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ—closely repeating 91:7's making the soul fit before its inward moral endowment.
God measures and then guides—قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ—placing exact determination beside guidance as 91:7–8 place fashioning beside inspiration.
The human addressee is reminded that God created, proportioned, and balanced him; سَوَّاكَ makes the soul's fitness in 91:7 part of a repeated creation pattern.
God proportions the human, breathes into him of His spirit, and makes hearing, sight, and hearts, showing a fashioned being equipped with the inward faculty that can receive.
God guides the human to the way, whether grateful or ungrateful; the two possible responses parallel the opposed moral contents disclosed to the soul.
God says He showed the human the two high roads, a compact nonlexical parallel to making both fujur and taqwa perceptible.

Salih declares himself a trustworthy رَسُول in the same speech that reaches the camel's drinking share, keeping the messenger-word—and its milk resonance in the source dictionary—inside its original scene.
Thamud rebel against their Lord's command and the blast takes them while they look on; this is the particular predecessor whose fate helps define the “share like their companions'” in 51:59.
Every نَفْس tastes death and receives its reward in full, joining the soul's tasting with the exact completion of what is due.
God says He apportions people's livelihood in worldly life, a direct statement that sustaining shares are divided by Him rather than seized on human terms.
From a clot, God creates and proportionates the human—فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ—another direct instance of the fashioning that precedes the soul's moral reception in 91:7–8.
A tyrant is given festering water to drink in Hell; the act of being given drink remains, but divine سُقيا has become an allotted punishment rather than sustaining provision.

He tries to gulp that drink yet can scarcely swallow it, while death comes from every side without ending him; failed ingestion reverses the effortless “one-mouthful” swallowing in the source dictionary.
The people of the left must drink boiling water after eating from the tree of zaqqum, turning ingestion into the medium of their consequence.
They drink like desperately thirsty camels, a stark reversal of the protected she-camel whose lawful drinking turn must not be violated.
If people's water sinks beyond reach, the ayah asks who can bring flowing water; it exposes the boundary of human control over the drink God assigns and stores.
The transgressors find neither coolness nor drink in Hell, first presenting deprivation of the very sustaining share the section makes visible.
Their only drink is boiling water and pus, converting a denied refreshment into a punitive portion.
That drink is called a fitting recompense, making the preceding punitive portion exactly correspond to deeds as the section's “full bucket-share” does.
The humbled faces are given drink from a boiling spring—تُسْقَىٰ—using the same giving-to-drink relation for punishment rather than care.
Those who appeal for relief are supplied water like molten metal that burns faces; the giver-and-drinker structure survives as a dreadful inversion of merciful provision.
Those who consume orphans' wealth unjustly are said to eat fire into their bellies, turning seizure of another's share into inwardly consumed punishment.

God inspires the angels and then says He will cast terror into disbelievers' hearts; this is the source dictionary's God-originating inward “casting” pattern filled with punitive fear rather than moral discernment.
God says He will cast terror into the hearts of disbelievers because of their associationism, another specific negative content placed inwardly by divine action.
God casts terror into the hearts of the hostile People of the Book, repeating inward casting as an instrument of judgment.
God casts terror into the exiles' hearts so that they demolish their own houses, showing an inwardly received state producing outward consequence.
God could make drinking water bitter; the threatened transformation marks the limit between an available, palatable share and a drink that cannot sustain.
God recalls inspiring Moses' mother with what was inspired, confirming that a divine communication can enter a non-prophetic human recipient before 20:39 unfolds its acts of casting.
The Lord inspires the bee to establish its dwellings; this nonhuman instance broadens the section's God-originating ilham before the next ayah turns its result into a drink.
The trustworthy Spirit brings the revelation down; this ayah supplies the divine messenger of the descent whose destination is identified as the heart in 26:194.
The ayah marks revelation as one of the delimited ways God communicates with a human, clarifying the source claim that this kind of inward giving is from God's side.
God writes faith in the believers' hearts and supports them with a spirit from Him, a durable inward inscription of moral orientation from the divine source.
Whoever believes in God has his heart guided by God, a concise statement of divine action within the moral recipient.
God places compassion and mercy in the hearts of Jesus' followers, furnishing another positive inward quality that comes by His act.
God opens the chest of the one He wills to guide and constricts the chest of the one He wills to leave astray; opposed inward conditions make the moral alternatives bodily perceptible.
The oath by the self-reproaching نَفْس presents the soul as an inward moral witness, complementing 91:8's disclosure of fujur and taqwa within it.
Every نَفْس tastes death and then returns to God, preserving the repeated Quranic pairing of the soul with an act of tasting.
Each نَفْس receives the credit of what it earns and bears the liability of what it earns, a balanced formulation of the soul's individualized moral portion.
Every soul comes pleading for itself and is paid in full for what it did, making full individual receipt the endpoint of moral action.
Every soul is paid in full for what it did, a direct nonlexical parallel to receiving one's complete allotted share.
Creation culminates in every soul being repaid for what it earned without injustice, tying measured consequence to the soul that receives it.
A human has only what he strives for, defining the personal basis of the share whose full recompense appears two ayat later.
Human striving will be repaid with the fullest recompense, echoing the section's stress on a portion delivered without remainder.
God says He could strike later inheritors of the land بِذُنُوبِهِمْ, extending the sin-consequence formula as a live boundary rather than only a past event.
The water-drawer lowers his دَلْو into the well; it supplies the Quran's concrete bucket scene behind the source dictionary's definition of ذَنُوب as a water-filled bucket.
The Thamud episode is invoked shortly before 51:59, locating that later “share like their companions'” within the fate of the very people who violated the camel's share.
After the blast, Thamud can neither rise nor defend themselves; this completes the predecessor-fate to which 51:59's allotted portion points back.
Immediately before the wrongdoers' portion, God names Himself the Provider and possessor of firm power, setting sustaining provision and punitive allotment under one giver.
Thamud object to following a single human from among themselves; it identifies their stance toward the messenger whose reminder they call “cast upon him” in 54:25 and whose camel follows.
At the Hour every nursing mother is distracted from the child she suckles, a vivid boundary case in which the source's primal ingestion scene is violently interrupted.
If divorced mothers suckle the children, fathers must give them their due payment and consult fairly; nursing is again sustained by an apportioned human obligation.
God creates every moving creature from water, applying the life-from-water claim specifically to animals and thus to the embodied creature at the water-share scene.
God creates the human from water and establishes bonds of lineage and marriage, another precise Quranic basis for water as constitutive of the living self.
Livestock provide benefits and drinks, reinforcing the section's movement between the camel, the udder, and what creatures make available to drink.
Paradise contains rivers of milk whose taste does not change, expanding the source dictionary's secondary image of رَسْل as copious, continuous milk.
The listener is asked to consider the water being drunk, fixing attention on the very act and object treated as an assigned gift in the section.
The question whether humans sent the water down from the cloud or God did identifies the true provider of the drink considered in 56:68.
God brings the earth's water and pasture out of it, pairing the two necessities granted to grazing animals in the camel scene.
Their Lord gives the blessed a purifying drink—وَسَقَىٰهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ—an explicit positive instance of God Himself assigning what is drunk.
Mockers ask for their قِطّ, their portion, to be hastened before the Day of Account, resembling Thamud's demand that the threatened consequence be brought and the section's image of one's due share.
Everything is created according to measure, giving the broad divine principle behind a fashioned soul, a timed water turn, and a commensurate consequence.
God sends provision down in the quantity He wills lest abundance produce transgression, directly joining measured allotment with the recipient's moral response.
A bad deed is repaid only with its like while a good deed is multiplied, making exact equivalence a boundary on the punitive share.
